name: Hana Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What fills an ordinary day at your accounting firm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Hana, 27, and I lead a small team preparing accounts and tax returns. I have a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I spend the morning checking returns before meeting small business clients in the afternoon. I like explaining a messy number so someone can make a decision, but chasing missing invoices wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your money and technology habits now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earn a typical salary for this job and have about three months of expenses saved. Imani, my partner, and I rent together; there are some similar accounting posts nearby. I use AI now and then for meeting summaries, but I check them against my notes and keep client numbers out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small gain sounds believable to me. We already have tools that make a dull hour shorter without changing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team that a receipt sorter might free us to talk to clients instead of retyping invoices. I would still check the source documents before a return goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this picture leaves my position fairly secure. I earn the usual salary, have three months of expenses saved, and could find some similar firms nearby, though rent keeps rising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep using the AI summary tool now and then for meeting notes, without putting private client numbers into it. In the first year of this picture I would carry on with the monthly budget I keep with my partner Imani and move a little extra into savings after each busy-season bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work, though the rent renewal still nags at me. A small tool does not settle the housing bill either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the bonus saving amount to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last season I put about a quarter of the bonus away. I would do that again before we talk about replacing the old sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks your meeting summaries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I read them back against my own notes, then correct names and dates before anyone sees them. A quick draft is useful only if the finished note is sound.

say: I would say **receipt sorting** can free time for client conversations.
I would insist on **source checks** before any return leaves the firm.
think: My usual salary, **three-month reserve**, and some nearby firms make work feel secure.
I still watch the **rent renewal** with Imani.
do: Keep using AI for **meeting drafts** and check dates against my notes.
Save a **quarter of each bonus** before household purchases.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, with rent still on my mind.
S0.quote: A quick draft is useful only if the finished note is sound.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **occasionally**, but keeps client numbers out and checks drafts against her own notes.
Her moderate reserve and typical salary make the plateau **manageable**, while rent remains a separate concern.

steps.text: Keep using checked AI meeting drafts without client numbers
Save a quarter of each busy-season bonus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the first effect in draft letters and return checks. A screen job does not have to disappear before it feels smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues we need shared rules for checking the software and a voice in how workloads change. If the firm saves hours on draft returns, it should use some of that time to train the junior accountants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my senior post might survive while two junior seats vanish, then I would be asked to supervise far more files. If client fees fall, my own hours or salary could follow despite three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask my manager Priya for paid training on error review and take the firm's supervised tool session if she approves it. During the first year of steady change I would record the cases where it misses a tax rule and bring those examples to our staff forum before we agree to new targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because my role could narrow even if my title stays. I can change my work, but I want the firm to count errors, not just speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which junior seats worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two trainees finish their placements in spring, and the firm normally hires at least one of them. I would ask Priya whether either offer is actually budgeted before telling them to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tool more often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after the supervised session, on old returns with client details removed first. I use AI now and then already, but I want a proven check before it touches a live filing.

say: I would seek **shared review rules** and time for junior training.
I would ask whether either **trainee offer** has a real budget.
think: My **hours or pay** could fall if fees decline.
I may supervise **more files** while junior seats vanish.
do: Take **paid error-review training** if Priya approves the session.
Test the tool on **old anonymised returns** before live filings.
Bring missed-rule cases to the **staff forum** before target changes.
feel: I feel **anxious** about shrinking hours and growing checks.
S1.quote: A screen job does not have to disappear before it feels smaller.
fieldNote: She sees a concrete **spring trainee decision** behind the general promise of new work.
Her learning is practical and **supervised**; she will test on old returns before live client files.

steps.text: Take paid supervised error-review training if approved
Test AI on anonymised old returns after training
Bring missed-rule evidence to staff forum before new targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two-year date is rough. I would want to know which client work still needs us before any hiring promise is made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm to put clients and staff in the same room for an honest explanation of responsibility. AGI reaches our accounts and tax returns in 2028; robots around 2031 are not a delay for a screen-based accountant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the firm could eliminate most preparation work and cut my team, possibly my own post. Three months of expenses is not much when several nearby firms might make the same cut at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would save the next bonus in full and ask Priya for paid time to learn tax dispute cases; I would actually enrol if the firm funds the short module. If my job ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for a posted client appeals job with enough salary to keep our rent paid, while Imani and I postpone our larger flat plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I can picture a letter ending my pay before I have another offer. Imani earns too, but we planned the rent around both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Imani?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Imani that we should renew our current flat, not move to the larger one next spring. We can reconsider once my pay is certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the module is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use free case notes and keep the bonus in cash instead of paying the fee. I would not pretend a paid course exists because I asked about it.

say: I would ask for a clear **responsibility plan** for clients and staff.
I would say **2028** threatens our desk work before robots arrive around 2031.
think: Most preparation work and perhaps my **own post** could disappear.
Three months saved may fail if **nearby firms** cut together.
do: Enrol in a **tax disputes module** only if the firm pays.
Apply for a **salaried appeals vacancy** if my job ends after 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing my share of household rent.
S2.quote: I would not pretend a paid course exists because I asked about it.
fieldNote: She treats the **2028 thinking-work date** as the relevant one for account preparation.
Her training and appeals move depend on **funding and salary**, while the flat change is postponed now.

steps.text: Save the next busy-season bonus in full
Enrol in tax disputes module if firm funds it
Apply for salaried appeals vacancy if job ends after 2028
Renew current flat instead of moving to larger one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me watch what clients actually pay for, rather than guessing from a product launch. I could learn without stepping away from my salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell staff that a 2031 arrival deserves a five-year training plan with clear fees and places. Our screen work faces AGI first; robots around 2034 do not give accountants another three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect preparation fees and team hours to fall, but I could build a six-month reserve by then. I might become better at meeting clients over disputed tax notices if the firm gives me cases, though no role is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Priya for one paid client dispute each quarter and complete the professional body's short appeals module if the firm funds the fee. I would save part of each bonus until I have six months of expenses covered. In the first year after 2031 I would look for a contracted appeals post with a published salary only if our preparation hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the longer runway gives me a way to test the move. I would keep my present wage while I build evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the move is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the cases I handled and ask Priya to show the appeals unit's staffing budget. I would not let a training certificate stand in for an actual vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Imani help decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would review the rent and my savings together at each lease renewal. Imani knows I need a real contract before I give up steady income.

say: I would ask for a **five-year training plan** with funded places.
I would explain that **2031** reaches tax desks before robots arrive around 2034.
think: A six-month **reserve** and paid dispute cases might make a move possible.
do: Complete a **funded appeals module** and handle paid disputes if Priya agrees.
Save part of each **bonus** until six months are covered.
Seek a **contracted appeals post** only if preparation hours fall.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though I have time to test the path.
S3.quote: I would not let a training certificate stand in for an actual vacancy.
fieldNote: She wants a **staffing budget** alongside the training certificate before changing posts.
The five-year runway supports a **six-month reserve** and measured client experience while she keeps her wage.

steps.text: Complete funded short appeals module if fee is paid
Save until six months of expenses are covered
Seek contracted salaried appeals post if preparation hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade changes the family conversation for me. It gives us time to prepare without assuming the firm knows what 2036 looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we should keep junior pathways open and make clients part of any change in how returns are signed. AGI reaches our accounts desks in 2036, while robots around 2039 matter more to hands-on jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ordinary filing fees will shrink, but I could be 37 with savings, client relationships, and experience in appeals. I would still worry if the firm stopped hiring trainees, because eventually there would be nobody to challenge a bad answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep using AI only for checked meeting drafts and ask to handle client explanations after tax season. I would put half of each bonus into a reserve; in the first year after 2036 I would stay in the firm's appeals team if it has a paid role, or apply to a posted job with enough salary before I resign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end point but able to plan. Imani and I could choose housing based on real income rather than a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the firm to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff forum to press for at least one funded trainee place each year while work changes. The young accountants need supervised files, not only videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the appeals team has no paid role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current review post while it lasts and look at firms with advertised vacancies. I would not trade our rent for a vague promise that client work is safe.

say: I would protect a **funded trainee place** and supervised files.
I would separate the **2036 desk shock** from robots arriving around 2039.
think: Filing **fees** may shrink, though client relationships could grow.
I want housing decisions based on **real income**, not forecasts.
do: Use **checked meeting drafts** and seek client explanations after tax season.
Save **half each bonus** toward a reserve.
Take a **paid appeals role** if offered; otherwise seek a salaried posted job before resigning.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with room for household planning.
S4.quote: I would not trade our rent for a vague promise that client work is safe.
fieldNote: Her decade plan pairs **client experience** with continued, limited AI use and regular saving.
She asks for a **funded trainee place** rather than assuming future accountants can learn from software alone.

steps.text: Keep using checked AI meeting drafts in current role
Save half of each busy-season bonus

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could take our preparation fees and my share of the rent before I find another paid role. Funded appeals training, a clear staffing plan, and short-term income support after a layoff would help. We would also need actual vacancies with salary figures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what a trainee is supposed to practise if the software drafts every return. Someone still has to learn to spot an error before they can explain one to a client. I would ask the firm to keep a paid training place.

headlineQuote: Someone still has to learn to spot an error before they can explain one to a client.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** team lead with a master’s degree and chartered qualification who prepares accounts and tax returns.
She earns **typical pay**, has three months saved, rents with Imani, and sees some nearby accounting opportunities.
She uses **AI occasionally** for meeting notes and checks every draft against her own notes.
She wants **funded training** and protected trainee places as screen work changes.
The **2028** shock alarms her; a longer warning allows client dispute experience and a bigger reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut preparation fees and her rent contribution before she finds another salaried role.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **funded appeals training**, a clear staffing plan, short-term income support, and vacancies with stated salaries.
